Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal :: Name :: chunk_0001
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/K%27inich_Janaab%27_Pakal.svg/250px-K%27inich_Janaab%27_Pakal.svg.png)](/wiki/File:K%27inich_Janaab%27_Pakal.svg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/PakalImage2a.jpg/250px-PakalImage2a.jpg)](/wiki/File:PakalImage2a.jpg)

Kʼinich Janaab Pakal I's glyphs.

Pakal's full name, *Kʼinich Janaab Pakal* ("Radiant Corn-Flower (?) Shield"[[5]](#cite_note-8)), is rendered in [Classic Maya](/wiki/Classic_Maya "Classic Maya") as **KʼINICH-JANA꞉B-PAKAL-la**, **KʼINICH-JANA꞉B-pa-ka-la**, or **KʼINICH-ja-na-bi-pa-ka-la**.[[6]](#cite_note-9) Before his name was securely deciphered from extant [Maya inscriptions](/wiki/Maya_script "Maya script"), Pakal had been known by various nicknames and approximations, including **Sun Shield** and **8 Ahau**.

In modern sources Pakal's name is also sometimes appended with a [regnal number](/wiki/Regnal_number "Regnal number"),[[N 4]](#cite_note-10) to distinguish him from other rulers with this name who either preceded or followed him in the dynastic lineage of Palenque. Confusingly, he has at times been referred to as *either* "Pakal I" or "Pakal II". Reference to him as Pakal II alludes to his maternal grandfather (died c. 612), who also bore the name [Janahb Pakal](/wiki/Janahb_Pakal "Janahb Pakal"). However, although his grandfather was a personage of *[ajaw](/wiki/Ajaw "Ajaw")* ranking, he does not himself appear to have been a king. When instead the name *Pakal I* is used, this serves to distinguish him from two later known successors to the American rulership, [Kʼinich Janaab Pakal II](/wiki/K%CA%BCinich_Janaab_Pakal_II "Kʼinich Janaab Pakal II") (ruled c. 742) and [Janaab Pakal III](/wiki/Janaab_Pakal_III "Janaab Pakal III"), the last-known Palenque ruler (ruled c. 799).[[7]](#cite_note-11)

[Branch Rickey](/wiki/Branch_Rickey "Branch Rickey"), president and general manager of the [Brooklyn Dodgers](/wiki/Brooklyn_Dodgers "Brooklyn Dodgers"), began making efforts to introduce a black baseball player to the previously all-white professional baseball leagues in the mid-1940s. He selected [Jackie Robinson](/wiki/Jackie_Robinson "Jackie Robinson") from a list of promising [Negro league](/wiki/Negro_league "Negro league") players. After obtaining a commitment from Robinson to "turn the other cheek" to any [racial antagonism](/wiki/Racial_antagonism "Racial antagonism") directed at him, Rickey agreed to sign him to a contract for $600 a month (equivalent to $9,906 in 2025). In what was later referred to as "The Noble Experiment", Robinson was the first black baseball player in the International League since the 1880s, joining the Dodgers' farm club, the [Montreal Royals](/wiki/Montreal_Royals "Montreal Royals"), for the 1946 season.[[61]](#cite_note-61)

The following year, the Dodgers called up Robinson to the major leagues. On April 15, 1947, Robinson made his major league debut at Ebbets Field before a crowd of 26,623 spectators, including more than 14,000 black patrons. Black baseball fans began flocking to see the Dodgers when they came to town, abandoning the Negro league teams that they had followed exclusively. Robinson's promotion met a generally positive, although mixed, reception among newspaper writers and white major league players. "Easy on Me" is 3 minutes and 44 seconds long.[[13]](#cite_note-Apple_Music-13) Kurstin produced the song and engineered it with Alex Pasco and Julian Burg. Kurstin plays [bass guitar](/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), kick drum, and piano. [Tom Elmhirst](/wiki/Tom_Elmhirst "Tom Elmhirst") helmed the song's [mixing](/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") at [Electric Lady Studios](/wiki/Electric_Lady_Studios "Electric Lady Studios") in New York, and [Randy Merrill](/wiki/Randy_Merrill "Randy Merrill") handled [mastering](/wiki/Mastering_(audio) "Mastering (audio)") at Sterling Sound in New Jersey.[[1]](#cite_note-Notes-1)

"Easy on Me" is a [torch](/wiki/Torch_song "Torch song") song and [ballad](/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad")[[14]](#cite_note-Still_No.1-14) which places emphasis on Adele's vocals over piano instrumentation.[[15]](#cite_note-NME_review-15) The song opens with a gentle piano, which intensifies as it progresses, leading into the vocals.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-17) Adele's voice mimics this according to *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*'s [Alexis Petridis](/wiki/Alexis_Petridis "Alexis Petridis"), as it "sounds initially wounded, then soars".[[17]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-17) The song almost completely eschews the use of percussion instruments,[[14]](#cite_note-Still_No.1-14)[[18]](#cite_note-18) but a bass drum and bass guitar are played during its latter half.[[19]](#cite_note-Telegraph_review-19) In the chorus, Adele delivers the song title in elongated [vocal runs](/wiki/Vocal_run "Vocal run") and stretches the "e" sound through eight different musical notes.[[19]](#cite_note-Telegraph_review-19) Mikael Wood of the *[Los Angeles Times](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* described her performance as "soaring yet slightly crinkly around the edges".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

The majority of the country borders water, including the [Skagerrak](/wiki/Skagerrak "Skagerrak") inlet to the south, the [North Sea](/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") to the southwest, the North [Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") ([Norwegian Sea](/wiki/Norwegian_Sea "Norwegian Sea")) to the west, and the [Barents Sea](/wiki/Barents_Sea "Barents Sea") to the north. It borders [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") to the east, and in the northeast it has land borders with [Finland](/wiki/Finland "Finland") and with [Russia](/wiki/Russia "Russia").
